quote.text: In every walk with nature, one receives far more than he seeks.
quote.author: John Muir

fun_fact.text: Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards! They can beat their wings up to 80 times per second, creating that characteristic humming sound. These tiny acrobats also have an incredible memory, remembering every flower they've visited and how long it will take for each to refill with nectar.

short_read.title: Why Do Trees Grow So Tall in the Pacific Northwest?
short_read.teaser: The Douglas firs and Western red cedars around Port Angeles reach extraordinary heights thanks to a perfect combination of mild winters, summer fog, and rich soil. Discover what makes the Olympic Peninsula a giant tree paradise.

medium_read.title: The Secret Lives of Orcas in the Salish Sea
medium_read.teaser: The orca pods that swim through the Strait of Juan de Fuca have distinct cultures, languages, and family traditions passed down through generations. Learn about the fascinating social world of these intelligent marine mammals that call your waters home.

long_read.title: Hungarian Folk Art: The Stories in the Stitches
long_read.teaser: Traditional Hungarian embroidery tells stories through intricate patterns, each region with its own distinctive style and meaning. This beautiful exploration reveals how generations of Hungarian women preserved their culture, identity, and artistry through needle and thread.

port_angeles.title: Black-Tailed Deer at Hurricane Ridge
port_angeles.description: August is a wonderful time to spot black-tailed deer at Hurricane Ridge, especially in the early morning or late afternoon. These gentle creatures are often seen grazing in the meadows alongside the wildflowers, and the fawns born in June are now old enough to explore with their mothers. The Olympic marmots are also very active this time of year!

puzzle_1.question: A hummingbird's heart beats approximately ___ times per minute.
puzzle_1.correct_response: Wonderful! That's right — 1,200 beats per minute! That tiny heart works incredibly hard to power such amazing flight.
puzzle_1.close_response: Very close! A hummingbird's heart beats about 1,200 times per minute — that's 20 times per second!
puzzle_1.wrong_response: A hummingbird's heart actually beats about 1,200 times per minute! That's incredibly fast — about 20 beats every single second to fuel their energetic lifestyle.
puzzle_1.learn_more_text: To put this in perspective, a human heart beats about 60-100 times per minute at rest. Hummingbirds need this rapid heartbeat to support their incredibly fast metabolism and hovering flight.

puzzle_2.question: Which Hungarian word means 'butterfly'?
puzzle_2.correct_response: Beautiful! Pillangó is indeed butterfly in Hungarian — such a lovely, poetic-sounding word!
puzzle_2.wrong_response: The Hungarian word for butterfly is 'pillangó' — doesn't it sound musical? (Virág means flower, madár means bird, and napraforgó means sunflower.)
puzzle_2.learn_more_text: The word 'pillangó' comes from an old Hungarian root meaning 'to flutter.' Many Hungarian nature words have similarly poetic origins, reflecting the deep connection between the language and the natural world.

puzzle_3.question: What type of tree can live for over 1,000 years in the Olympic National Forest?
puzzle_3.correct_response: Yes! Western red cedars can live well over 1,000 years in the Olympic Peninsula. Some ancient cedars near Port Angeles are estimated to be 1,200 years old — they were saplings when Vikings were sailing!
puzzle_3.wrong_response: The answer is Western red cedar! These magnificent trees can live over 1,000 years in the Olympic forests. Some ancient cedars growing near Port Angeles were already hundreds of years old when European explorers first arrived.
puzzle_3.learn_more_text: Western red cedars were sacred to Coast Salish peoples, who called them 'the tree of life.' They used every part — the rot-resistant wood for longhouses and canoes, the bark for clothing and baskets, and the roots for rope.
